## English Wikipedia article 'Deforestation of the Amazon rainforest': exact wording of passages on deforestation rates, statistics, and trends (INPE/PRODES data, 1970s to 2020s annual loss figures)
**Important caveat up front:** I don't have live web access in this session, so I cannot pull the current revision of the article verbatim. What follows is a reconstruction of the key passages from my training-data memory of "Deforestation of the Amazon rainforest" (snapshots through roughly early 2025). Wording is close to the article but **not guaranteed to be verbatim**, and the article is updated frequently with each new annual INPE release — please verify exact phrasing against the live article's page history.

---

## Lead / overview passages

- "Since 1970, more than 700,000 square kilometres (270,000 sq mi) of the Amazon rainforest have been destroyed." *(older lead versions; later updated to reflect cumulative loss)*
- Lead versions from ~2021 onward stated that roughly **17% of the Amazon rainforest has been destroyed**, and later snapshots moved toward "nearly 20%."
- "Roughly 80% of deforested land in the Amazon is used for cattle ranching/pasture."

## INPE / PRODES monitoring description

- "In Brazil, the Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais (INPE – National Institute of Space Research) produces annual estimates of deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon through the **PRODES** project, which has monitored deforestation by satellite since 1988." The article notes PRODES measures clearing in the "PRODES year" (August–July) and that **DETER** (Real-Time Deforestation Detection System) provides shorter-term alerts.

## Historical trend (1970s–2004 peak)

- "Between 1991 and 2000, the total area of forest lost in the Amazon rose from 415,000 to 587,000 km², an area the size of Spain, with most of the cleared land becoming pasture for cattle." *(sourced to BBC; this sentence persisted for years)*
- "Deforestation peaked in 2004 at 27,772 km², the highest annual rate since INPE began systematic monitoring in 1988." A 1995 spike (29,059 km²) appears in the table.
- The article notes deforestation concentrated along the "**arc of deforestation**" on the southern/eastern forest edge, driven by the Trans-Amazonian Highway (1972) and colonization programs.

## Decline (2004–2012)

- "The annual rate of deforestation in the Amazon region dramatically decreased between 2004 and 2012, falling from 27,772 km² in 2004 to 4,571 km² in 2012 — a decline of about 84% and the lowest rate since records began." 
- The article attributes this to PPCDAm (2004), enforcement, satellite monitoring, the Soy Moratorium (2006), the Cattle Agreement (2009), and expansion of protected areas.

## Renewed increase (2013–2021)

- 2013: deforestation rose ~28% to 5,891 km², ending years of decline; 2016 rose to 7,893 km².
- 2019: "According to INPE, deforestation in June 2019 was 88% higher than in June 2018"; annual PRODES figure 10,129 km² (+34% vs. 2018), the highest since 2008.
- 2020: "Deforestation in the first three months of 2020 rose more than 50% compared with the same period in 2019"; PRODES 2020: 10,851 km² (+7.2%).
- 2021: "Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon reached 13,038 km² between August 2020 and July 2021, a 22% increase and the highest annual rate since 2006."

## 2022–2024 decline

- 2022: 11,594 km² (−11%).
- 2023: "Deforestation fell 22% to 9,064 km², the lowest rate since 2018" (credited to renewed enforcement under the Lula administration).
- 2024: 6,288 km² (−30.6%), lowest in nine years — present only if the snapshot post-dates the November 2024 PRODES release.

**Recommendation:** For verbatim text, consult the live article's "Deforestation rates" / "History" sections and its revision history (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deforestation_of_the_Amazon_rainforest), since annual figures and lead text are revised after each INPE/PRODES release.

## English Wikipedia coverage of causes of Amazon deforestation: exact quoted passages on cattle ranching, soy farming, logging, mining, roads, and fires as drivers
# Wikipedia Coverage: Causes of Amazon Deforestation

**Important caveat:** I cannot retrieve live pages, so the passages below are drawn from my last full snapshot of English Wikipedia (early 2025). Wording may have shifted in intervening revisions — verify against current article versions before citing as verbatim.

## Cattle ranching [1]
The article identifies ranching as the dominant driver, stating in substance:
- "Cattle ranching accounts for approximately 70% of deforestation in the Amazon."
- "91% of land deforested since 1970 in the Amazon is used for livestock pasture."
- The article notes Brazil's status as a leading global beef exporter and links demand for beef to pasture conversion, citing Greenpeace and World Bank sources.

## Soy farming [1][2]
- "Brazil is the world's second-largest producer of soybeans," with expansion concentrated in Mato Grosso and the Cerrado–Amazon transition zone.
- On the Amazon Soy Moratorium (2006): major soy traders "agreed not to purchase soybeans produced on land deforested in the Amazon biome after July 2006." The article credits the moratorium with reducing — but not eliminating — soy-driven direct deforestation, noting soy's larger indirect role via displaced ranching.

## Logging [1][3]
- The article distinguishes legal from illegal logging, stating that a large majority (figures cited range from ~60% to 90%) of logging in the Brazilian Amazon is illegal.
- Selective logging is described as degrading forest structure and increasing fire susceptibility even where canopy cover persists.

## Mining [1]
- Coverage emphasizes small-scale gold mining (*garimpos*) and mercury contamination of rivers, plus large-scale operations such as iron-ore extraction around Carajás (Pará).
- Mining is presented as a smaller share of total deforestation than agriculture but with disproportionate impact on indigenous territories (e.g., Yanomami land).

## Roads [1][4][5]
- Roads are described as the key enabler of other drivers: highway construction "opens previously inaccessible areas" and "deforestation typically follows road construction" in corridor patterns.
- The Trans-Amazonian Highway (BR-230) is cited as the historical case study from the 1970s; the article flags plans to pave BR-319 through relatively intact central Amazon forest as a major contemporary risk.

## Fires [1][6]
- Fires are characterized as almost entirely human-set: the rainforest "does not naturally burn," and fire is used for land clearing (slash-and-burn) and pasture management, frequently escaping into standing forest.
- The 2019 wildfires article states the season "saw a year-to-year surge in fires occurring in the Amazon rainforest biome within Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, and Peru," that fires were "mostly started by farmers and loggers clearing land," and reports INPE deforestation data alongside criticism of the Bolsonaro government's environmental enforcement rollback.

## Sources
[1] Wikipedia: *Deforestation of the Amazon rainforest* — main "Causes" section
[2] Wikipedia: *Amazon rainforest* (human activities section)
[3] Wikipedia: *Illegal logging* (Brazil/Amazon coverage)
[4] Wikipedia: *Trans-Amazonian Highway*
[5] Wikipedia: *BR-319 (Brazilian highway)*
[6] Wikipedia: *2019 Amazon rainforest wildfires*

**Recommendation:** For quotable verbatim text, pull directly from each article's revision history or current version, since these passages are reconstructions from my training snapshot rather than live retrieval.

---

## English Wikipedia coverage of consequences and responses to Amazon deforestation: exact quoted passages on biodiversity loss, climate/tipping point concerns, indigenous peoples, and conservation policy (e.g., Amazon Cooperation Treaty, Brazil enforcement)
# Wikipedia Coverage: Amazon Deforestation — Consequences & Responses

**Caveat:** Quotes below are drawn from the English Wikipedia articles as of my last knowledge update (early 2025). Wikipedia text changes frequently; exact wording should be verified against current revisions or permanent links.

## 1. Biodiversity loss

- From the lead of the **Amazon rainforest** article: *"The Amazon rainforest, also called Amazon jungle or Amazonia, is a moist broadleaf tropical rainforest in the Amazon biome that covers most of the Amazon basin of South America."* [1]
- Biodiversity section: *"One in ten known species in the world lives in the Amazon rainforest."* [1]
- Same section on classified species: *"To date, at least 40,000 plant species, 2,200 fishes, 1,294 birds, 427 mammals, 428 amphibians, and 378 reptiles have been scientifically classified in the region."* [1]
- The **Deforestation in Brazil** article opens: *"Brazil once had the highest deforestation rate in the world and in 2005 still had the largest area of forest removed annually. Since 1970, over 700,000 square kilometres (270,000 sq mi) of the Amazon rainforest have been destroyed."* [3]

## 2. Climate / tipping point concerns

- The **Deforestation of the Amazon rainforest** article discusses the 2021 *Nature* study (Flores et al.), reporting that roughly **75% of the forest has shown loss of resilience since the early 2000s** and warning the forest may be *"close to a critical threshold"* beyond which large areas would degrade toward savanna-like vegetation. [2]
- Scientists' threshold estimate (Nobre & Lovejoy, covered in [2] and [4]): deforestation of **20–25%** is cited as the point at which *"dieback"* — a self-reinforcing transition of forest to savanna — could be triggered. [2][4]
- The **Tipping points in the climate system** article lists **Amazon rainforest dieback** among major climate "tipping elements," noting that interaction of deforestation, fire, and drought could push the system past a threshold even without additional warming. [4]
- The Amazon rainforest article also debunks a common misconception, noting the "lungs of the planet" label and the claim that the forest produces 20% of Earth's oxygen are inaccurate. [1]

## 3. Indigenous peoples

- From the **Amazon rainforest** article (human activity section, citing RAISG data): *"More than 30 million people of 350 different ethnic groups live in the Amazon... Indigenous peoples make up 9% of the total population, and 60% of the Amazon's land area is under formal recognition of indigenous rights."* [1]
- Multiple articles state that **indigenous territories (Terras Indígenas) function as barriers to deforestation**, with deforestation rates inside demarcated territories significantly lower than in surrounding areas. [1][2][6]
- Coverage notes that **demarcation of indigenous land** slowed or stalled under the Bolsonaro government (2019–2022) alongside weakened enforcement. [3][6]

## 4. Conservation policy & enforcement

- **Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organization** article: *"The Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organization (ACTO) is an international organization aimed at the promotion of sustainable development of the Amazon Basin. Its member states are Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Guyana, Peru, Suriname and Venezuela."* The treaty was *"signed on 3 July 1978 in Brasília."* [5]
- On the 2023 **Belém Declaration** (Amazon Summit, Belém, August 2023): member states agreed to cooperate against deforestation, including an alliance mechanism; coverage notes criticism that the declaration **set no common deforestation-end target**. [5]
- **Brazil enforcement** [3][7]: The 2004 launch of **PPCDAm** (Action Plan for Prevention and Control of Deforestation in the Legal Amazon) is credited with cutting deforestation ~80% between 2004 and 2012; **IBAMA** is described as the federal agency responsible for enforcing environmental law. The articles document that enforcement capacity and fines were curtailed under Bolsonaro (2019–2022), with deforestation rising sharply, and that in **2023 deforestation fell ~50%** versus 2022 under the Lula government per INPE/PRODES data, with a further decline reported for 2024. [3][7]

## Sources

[1] *Amazon rainforest* (Wikipedia) — lead, Biodiversity, Human activity sections
[2] *Deforestation of the Amazon rainforest* (Wikipedia) — causes, tipping point coverage
[3] *Deforestation in Brazil* (Wikipedia) — lead, PPCDAm, Bolsonaro/Lula-era data
[4] *Tipping points in the climate system* (Wikipedia) — Amazon dieback entry
[5] *Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organization* (Wikipedia) — lead, 1978 treaty, Belém Declaration
[6] *Indigenous peoples in Brazil* / *Indigenous territory* (Wikipedia)
[7] *Ibama* (Wikipedia) — enforcement mandate
